title: Shift Register
body:
Made up of a bunch of cascading [[Flip-Flop]] circuits

Each flip-flop's $Q$ feeds the next one's $D$, so on every clock edge the whole contents
move one position along. That single behaviour gives you several things:

- **Serial to parallel.** Clock bits in one at a time, then read all $n$ outputs at once.
  This is the receive half of a [[UART]].
- **Parallel to serial.** Load all $n$ bits at once, then clock them out one at a time.
  The transmit half.
- **Shifting as arithmetic.** Shift left is multiply by 2, shift right is divide by 2,
  which is where the `lsl` / `lsr` instructions come from.

The first two are why [[Serial I-O]] needs one at each end: the wire carries bits, the
[[CPU]] wants words, and the shift register is the conversion.

**Feed the output back in and it becomes a keystream generator.** A *linear feedback shift
register* takes the XOR of a few chosen cells as the next input bit, so it cycles through
$2^n - 1$ states before repeating and produces a bit stream that looks random. That is the
classic hardware [[Stream Cipher]] in [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111), and it is the one place a
4th-year maths course lands directly on this note. It is also the reason "linear" is in the name
and a warning: being linear, it is solved by $2n$ known output bits, so a real cipher combines
several of them non-linearly.
